utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning to everyone. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Alex Demirdjian for the Prosecution, with Tom Hannis, Crispian Smith, and our legal intern, Thomas Hughes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Ms. Melody Whittaker, and Ms. Claire Plumb appearing for Stanisic Defence this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dragan Krgovic and Aleksandar Aleksic appearing for Zupljanin Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Demirdjian, we've been alerted to an application that will be made or is about to be made before we proceed with this mornings's first witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. And if we could go in private session for a moment to address this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If you're satisfied, sir, with the particulars on that sheet, would you please sign it and hand it back to the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It must be the change of climate. That's why I'm coughing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and [Microphone not activated] marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P1673, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, we mean no disrespect when we refer to you as Mr. Witness or by the number that has been assigned to you as a pseudonym. It's just that the -- having regard to the protective measures that have been afforded, that is the way in which -- that is the most practical way to proceed. Now in addition to what would have told us already, could you tell us what your profession is or was and what your ethnicity is and what your date of birth is ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yeah. We would go into private session for this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, before we move on, if I'm not wrong, this witness is called for the limited purpose of covering adjudicated facts 500 to 505; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In addition, there are also four adjudicated facts that were challenged by the Defence, 1214, which the witness just dealt with. 1215. 1218. I believe there was 1216 as well, though I'm not sure this was properly challenged, so let's just say 1214, 1215, and 1218 are the additional facts that he will be dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. But then in the ones I mentioned, 500 to 505 --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- you do realise that four of them already taken judicial notice of.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I understand the ones that have a line through them are the ones that we will be dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: A line through.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Well, in the adjudicated facts 500 to 503 in the decision they're all in one fact, and there's a line through specific facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So that's what I will be dealing with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, we are now in public session, I will ask you to be careful not to identify yourself when speaking. You told us that your street name changed, and I will not be saying the names of the streets, but when did that change occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was before any combat activity, when -- when the texts was changed from Latinic script to Cyrillic script, and also they changed the street names. That was before any combat activities so before April.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now you told us earlier that you were dismissed from the police and then you went home. Could you explain to the Trial Chamber very briefly what you did during this time, after you were dismissed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing. I moved about freely. I monitored the situation. I watched TV, and I could tell that things are not going to come out right. And then there was a curfew that was introduced in April between 10.00 in the evening and 7.00 in the morning, or 6.00 in the morning. So it wasn't easy. On one occasion I was stopped at a check-point. There they were check-points with machine-gun nests also at all major routes towards Banja Luka, Doboj, Batajnica. So that kind of things were happening. And we would get together and discuss what was going on. We just couldn't figure it out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it is an admitted fact in this case that a takeover took place in the municipality of Teslic around the 3rd or the 4th of June, 1992. Now, what I want to deal with is a time when you were arrested. Could you tell the Trial Chamber when did that occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was arrested on the 5th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who arrested you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A group of people came I don't -- didn't know in camouflage uniforms with white belts. According to me, they were military policemen, because that's the kind of uniform military policemen used to wear. There was five, six, or seven of them. I can't remember. They were looking for me. I was planning to take my rifle back and hand it in after the curfew but they came before I did so. They came with a red van and they called out to me. I said, yes, and they asked me to come down. They wanted to ask me something. And immediately when I came down and asked them, What is it? They started hitting me. They brought me down to the ground. My mother came to me but they pushed her away and leaned her against a wall. One of them had a bayonet and put it under her throat, kept it there for a few minutes. They beat me up. They didn't tie me up and they just threw me into the van. They asked me where the weapons were, the automatic rifle and the five cartridges of ammunition. They told me that, today, on -- or that day was the last day when one should hand in the weapons. Two or three of them went upstairs and took the semi-automatic gun, they put me in the van, and they took me to the SUP building. They said that I would be killed if they determined that someone has fired from my rifle. They sent rifle to Banja Luka. They put me in the detention unit in the police station, and I saw that there were many people I knew, officials, my colleagues. It was full, this detention unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us at the beginning that you were planning to take your rifle back. Was this announced in any way? Why were you planning to return it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A neighbour of mine, a husband of a relative of mine, Mr. Aco Kovacevic who was an official in the local commune before, he told me that it was broadcast over the radio that all the weapons need to be handed in by the 5th of June, that that's the deadline. And I said okay. And I said let's go together, and my brother would drive me there. So I asked him can you come to my place at about 8.00 and then we'll see what happens because I was told earlier that I could keep the weapons, but these guys came half an hour, maybe an hour before we were due to leave and they took me away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And without giving the specifics of the location, just to clear this up for the Trial Chamber, you told us earlier that you had an apartment in town and you had a house 3 kilometres away from the town of Teslic. Where were you when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in my house, which is 3 kilometres away from the town proper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, you told us that you were taken to the police station and you were held there. Where exactly were you held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was held in the cells that we had in the police station. This is the building adjacent to the building of the police station in the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we pull up 65 ter 10557, please. Your Honours, I'm about to use a few of the photographs we took during the site visit. I hope that there's no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, can you see this photograph on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what are we looking at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the police station, where I used to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And the cells that you told us are not in this building; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Or, rather, yes. My brother was held in the last room on the left-hand side in this building later on, when they brought him in. That's where the police weapons used to be kept. And my brother was held there for about five or six days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about yourself, were you held in this building? I will repeat that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just before we move away from this picture, can you tell us, in this building we see a number of windows. To your knowledge, who worked in those offices?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean earlier, when it was the time when government was normal or during this pre-war activity period?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about, if you know, during the time of your arrest or shortly prior to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To the right, ground floor, these were the offices of the duty officers. Above them was the crime department offices. And above that, was a meeting room. On the left-hand side, the first room was the waiting-room. And from that waiting-room, you go into a corridor, and there were the offices for IDs and passports, and a woman used to work there. Never mind. And above that was with a clerk in charge of weapons. And, at the end, there was this room where we kept ammunition and weapons but where later they put detainees. And then the three rooms above that was the crime department. The first one was the head, and then on the top floor was the commander's assistant and then behind it was the communications centre, where I used to work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May I ask for this document to be admitted, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have no objection. The Trial Chamber visited the location. We have photos of all the rooms. I don't know what the purpose is. And, also, this photo is not on the 65 ter list. We didn't have notice about it. Or maybe ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, is it right that not one of your documents on your document list is on the 65 ter list?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: These are all the photos from the site visit, indeed, Your Honours. I don't know if there's an issue of notice here or if anybody has an objection, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I have a problem, Mr. Demirdjian, in that a site visit is to elucidate for the benefit of -- especially the Trial Chamber but for everyone, the evidence that has been already been heard. And whatever site visit is, it is not an occasion to receive evidence. I know that we did take photographs, extensive photographs, of the areas that we saw, and -- but -- and I confess a measure of uncertainty, as to the evidential status of this material, but I think it is fairly well settled that it would not be -- that the site visit would not have been a vehicle for receiving evidence. So although there is no objection, as such, from the Defence, and although, I suppose, it could be powerfully argued that no harm is done, I have grave reservations about giving this material the status of evidence because it is sort of out of -- out of kilter with the -- what we understand the purpose of the site visit to be. I remain open to be persuaded to the contrary, but instinctively, I would say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am aware that there is a lot of material that came through the site visit, and I do believe there is certain things such as comments and records that we made that should not be considered as evidence. Inasmuch as these images assist us in understanding the testimony of this witness, I don't think that there's a general rule that bars us from admitting photos that we took during that visit. It is not -- as I said, it is not something substantive in of itself. If you don't believe that these photos can assist, you there's a number of photos that will come, that I would seek to use as well, which my assist us in understanding, for example where the witness was, from which angle he was able to see certain things, especially when we get to his detention in the cell. I could deal with it without the photos, but I think it would help us to have them. So, I don't have -- yeah. But again, I don't think there's a general rule barring us from using these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Does counsel for Mr. Stanisic have a view on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not objecting to having these photos shown to the witness, but I don't see why the photos should be admitted. There already are photographs that are on the 65 ter list, and this just makes the total sum of evidence larger. I don't mind that the witness is shown the photographs, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one last thing if I may add. Rule 89 does allow you to admit any evidence that you consider to be relevant or have probative value, so if that can assist in this determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We are wondering, Mr. Demirdjian, why is there no application, then, to have them on the 65 ter, so then we could consider it and take a decision on it. This seems a little bit awkward as --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- procedurally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours, and I thought that I would make the application orally to not to burden ourselves again with motions which deal really with what are photographs. So I considered it not to be -- to be an issue that we could have raised orally. Again, as I said, I could continue without them. It's just for the purpose of illustration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, whereas we share your concern about overburdening the -- this -- this hearing with motions, we think that out of an abundance of caution such new photographs -- when I say new, those photographs taken on the site visit, which, in your estimation could be helpful should be identified in advance and listed in an application to include it in the 65 ter list, then we would be back on track procedurally as to the channel for moving these items in as evidence. But, the -- as I said, whereas there is merit in your argument about a motion without notice on your feet, we are a bit unsure as to where that might lead us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Well, Your Honours, what we could do for the time being, if you wish for us to file a motion, is at the moment we can mark these documents for identification, we could file a motion afterwards, and we will make sure that for future photographs if any need to be used we will file a motion in advance. And if you don't want to deliberate on the matter right away, we could at least mark them for identification. But the witness can actually talk about the photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Well, in as much as the witness is on the stand, we have the photograph in front of us, I suppose it could be marked for identification at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So I will seek to mark this document for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So the photograph may be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P1674, marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, could we pull up the next photograph which is 10558, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you will see a new photograph appear on the screen in a moment. Very well. Do you recognise this building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell the Trial Chamber what this building was used for prior to the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here, on the left, the entrance was the entrance to the premises of the ham radio enthusiasts. And then in this building there was also the -- there were the offices of the municipal committee and the municipal bodies. There were the information offices. On the right, there were apartments but they were turned into offices. The second entrance from the satellite dish is the entrance to the remand prison which was in the basement. And upstairs a colleague of mine lived. There's another entrance from the front; we can't see it in this photograph right now. An entrance from back side was also made. That led to the ID and passport department of the SUP.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this is the building you told us you were detained in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us that the second entrance is the entrance to the remand prison, which was in the basement. And is that where you were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first entrance from here. It's not the one above which there's a satellite dish, but the other which can be only seen poorly. There are two plaques above it, one white and one blue; that's the entrance that leads down to the basement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, who took you to this cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My colleague. Letic is his last name. I can't remember his first name, but he remained in service during the war. He was a young police officer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were guarding the premises?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were no guards down there. We were locked up, and we were behind metal doors, and there were also bars, in addition. But down there, there were no guards. The guards were at the entrance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who was guarding at the entrance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly reserve police officers, or active servicemen. They would walk to and fro between the two buildings, this one and the police station. And at any given moment, there were about a dozen police officers there, either active or reserve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And before I move away from the prison cell, could you tell us, what were the conditions of detention inside the cell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I got there, it was disastrous. People were all beaten up, 12 bloody, and I was appalled. I couldn't believe it when I entered. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were detained with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's difficult to say. Both rooms were full. One was -- the size of one was about 6 by 6 metres, and the other was actually a restroom. There were very many of us. Only the injured ones were allowed to lie down; otherwise there wasn't enough room for all of us to lie down. So many of us had to stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, if I might interrupt briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, one of the things that I neglected to mention when I was asking the introductory questions of you was our procedure in terms of the breaks, and for -- both for technical reasons, that is, having regard to the recording system and also to allow for the convenience of witnesses, we do not sit for longer than an hour and a half, and the Court's day ends at 1.45 because we have to make the courtroom available for another trial. We are scheduled to take our first break at 10.25, which is in eight minutes. But notwithstanding the fixed breaks that we have, and I'm mindful of what you would have indicated earlier about the respiratory difficulties you're having, if at any point you need a break, if you would indicate that to us, we would certainly accommodate you. So if you are able to continue for the next eight minutes, then we would have a 20-minute break and we would come back to resume your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my condition certainly won't improve. I started coughing yesterday. It must be the change of the climate and the humid air here. I can continue. I understand that it may bother you, but I can turn my head when I have to cough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It doesn't bother us. We are concerned about your comfort and convenience, sir. Sorry, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, to my knowledge we have a medical personnel in the building so maybe during the break maybe the witness can be escorted to the doctor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, if that would assist. Thank you -- thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I can wrap up this topic in the next few minutes and then we can take the break for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, sir. Let me see where I was. Right. Now you told us that the room was 6 by 6. And you told us both rooms were full. Just to clarify for the Trial Chamber, going down to the basement, which cell were you detained in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in the first cell by the entrance, and I was standing below the window, one of the windows where there were bars. And sometimes I would hold on to these bars and occasionally I would squat down because the room was full of urine, so you couldn't sit or lie there, and we were all bothered by the stench, the ammoniac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you were telling us that you were standing below the window. What did you see through this window? What were you -- were you able to see, first of all, through this window?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they allowed some air in, I was in a position to see everything. Bringing people in, beating them. I couldn't see it, but I heard them moaning and groaning. But when they beat up people outside, then I could see everything. I could the state they were in, and I looked upon all that went on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of such an occurrence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they were beating Mujo Zukanovic, he was a white collar crime inspector, we looked on. When they were beating Kopic, also known as Rambo, we also all looked on. (redacted) (redacted). And when they were beating Remzija Jasarevic we also watched that and so on. I don't know what you want to hear, but anyway they were beating people there. They lined up the police and the police beat them, even Miroslav Pijunovic, he broke off a bough from a nearby tree and used it to beat Rambo. Later they took him away behind the committee building and we never saw him again. Later on, I heard that he was killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And the last question before the break, you told us about seeing Rambo being beaten by Pijunovic. Who else was present during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what has this line of questioning to do with the adjudicated facts for which the witness has been called?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this witness is called to deal with his detention in the police station and what he witnessed there. This was my last question on the topic before moving on to the next building where he was held, and it's just fair enough to let him tell us what the conditions were during his detention and what he was able to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this witness has been called here to testify as to where he was detained, and that's all. And the Prosecutor, for the last ten or 15 minutes, has been asking questions about who was beating who.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: 5 -- 504, Mr. Krgovic. Just as one example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. But it says that they were detained but there's no mention of the conditions or individual incidents. And the adjudicated fact reads, 504: "As of 3 June 1992, civilians Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats were detained by the Bosnian Serbs, members of the military police and the civilian police, and members of the reserve police forces and paramilitary units." That's all the -- that's mentioned in this adjudicated fact. Individual incidents are not mentioned and nor are individual persons who were beaten. The Prosecutor is supposed to question the witness about these adjudicated facts, so there should be only one question about who provided security, and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Except, Mr. Krgovic, as a matter of sheer logic, if that is all that is led, then the impression could be had that it was a benign detention, whereas, what the questions that have been elicited so for point out is that it was not. So it strikes me that it is within the context of what is -- the fact in respect of which the witness is being called on to testify. Please proceed, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you just finish your answer in telling us who was present during the beating of Mr. Kopic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was beaten by Miroslav Pijunovic, also known Piko, and others who belonged to the so-called Red Berets and also reserve police officers. All of them beat him. They were standing in a circle around him, they beat him with hands and feet, and later he was even tied to a tree. All of them beat him with hands, feet, sticks, some of them -- he was a rather strong guy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, Your Honours. I have an intervention to the transcript. Could the witness repeat his first sentence, slowly, who exactly it was who beat this person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The group leader, Miroslav Pijunovic, also known as Piko, he beat him, and later on everybody else did. He even lined up the police and then he was taken to that lineup and then everybody beat him. Predrag Markocevic and Kuzmanovic, the chief of the SUP, watched. They were standing in the staircase watching and laughing, Marinko Djukic, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honour, I -- maybe I will ask for official correction from the transcript. What the witness said doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise, but what is this objection? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the better part -- the better part of the witness's answer has not been entered. Because he was explaining what would have happened with -- with the policemen who didn't beat this person in the lineup.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's let the witness answer again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, it appears that part of your answer was not entered in the transcript. Could you please perhaps repeat your answer slowly so that it makes it in the official transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were many of them in front of the police station, there was much coming and going anyway. So a lot of people were out there, and one of the leaders - at least I think he was one of the leaders - was Miroslav Pijunovic. He was very active in repression, he beat who he wanted to, and he was the first one to beat him with a stick, with his feet, and his hands. Later, the other members of the so-called Red Berets beat him. I don't know all their names. I know some of them but they were not present then. Then they lined up the police officers who were present, and then he was led between the two lines of police officers and they would all beat him with their hands or feet or sticks if they had any. So he had to walk through once, and once again, and then he was tide up. And then Miroslav Pijunovic broke off one of the boughs, then he removed the twigs and used that bough to beat him on the back and on his legs after which he fell on the ground, and then they untied him. They took him to the building and, that is, they took him behind the building and I don't know what happened later. We didn't see him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This may be a convenient time, Your Honours. Just before, perhaps we can also mark for identification the picture that's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, so marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit P1675, marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's 10.30. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is being brought in, I just wanted to inquire as to the matter of the material from the site visit and the way we were hoping to deal with it. I know that in other trials the bulk of the material was admitted in evidence at one stage of the case. I don't know what the plans were in this trial, whether Your Honours were expecting the parties to submit a motion because in relation to these photos, I was wondering if it is better to deal with it in bulk or have small motions to add them to the 65 ter list. I don't know if there's any -- anything has been thought about in this ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, thank you for that question. We will give it some consideration and we trust that we have will have an answer -- a definitive answer for you by the end of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, are you able to continue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before I continue with the next topic, I want to go back to something you told us during the first part day. At page 16 of the transcript we were talking about, if you remember, the street names and they told us that they changed from Latin to Cyrillic. I failed to ask you at that time what did those new signs look like, the new signs in Cyrillic that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The usual, blue boards with white lettering, I think. In Cyrillic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Regular.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you actually know who made those changes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was done by a utility company, Rad, from Teslic. They were ordered to do so by the authorities of the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, we were talking about your detention in the cells of the SJB building. How many days were you held there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Five days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in relation to the other detainees that were held with you, could you tell the Court what was their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, what happened to you after those five days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One day a bus parked in front of the prison building at the entrance. There were two policemen there. Not our guys. I think military policemen. They let us board the buses. Initially, I thought they were taking to us to Pribinic, but they were actually taking us toward the town proper and they brought us to the Territorial Defence Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the distance between the police station and the TO warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, maybe 500 or 600 metres. Less than a kilometre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what happened when you were brought to the Territorial Defence Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you were brought there. What -- what happened immediately when you were taken there? Were you taken somewhere in the building or ... if you can describe that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The bus stopped in front of this warehouse, the TO warehouse. It had a wide gate with two doors, which were -- the gates were open, and then they got us in, into this warehouse for -- or depot for weapons, but it was already empty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And when you say "us," how many of you were detained there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One bus full of people, so 40 to 60 people. And then it went back and brought another group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did more people -- were more people brought in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were people coming all the time in groups of five, ten, 15, day and night, 24 hours a day, they would be bringing people in who were, allegedly, scheduled to be exchanged. I don't know what was going on. We would never see them again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long were you detained in the TO warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was detained there until August. So June, July. I was released in August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at the height of it, what was the highest number of detainees that were held there at one time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What do you mean? How many of us were there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Initially you told us that there was two busloads of 40 to 60 people and told us that the numbers increased. What was the highest number of people detained there throughout your time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in the first day or two there was 200 or more than 200 of us there. I didn't count the heads. But it was a big space, so there was enough space for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we pull up P1349, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And while we are pulling up the picture, sir, could you tell us who was detained in the TO warehouse, if you recognise anyone, and who else was detained with you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: First of all, I believe I have a note here saying that P1349 was under seal. So perhaps if we could not broadcast it in the public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, sir, and I apologise for interrupting. I don't want you to list all the names of the people who were held there. Perhaps a better question to ask would be what was the ethnic background of those that were held with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were Croats and Muslims. There were five or six colleagues of mine there as well, policemen, active-duty policemen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there any specific characteristic of those who were detained there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what you're referring to again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, it's -- my question, it's maybe a little vague. What I meant to say is you told us there were Croats and Muslims detained there. And what I'm seeking from you is to explain to the Trial Chamber what kind of Croats and Muslims were held there, were they from a certain class of society or so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah, yes. Most of the people there, either policemen, then there was the bank manager, the president of the Executive Board, the president of the municipality, Seho Topcagic, people who held various positions. My opinion is that what they wanted was to remove them. And then there was a jeweller there who occasionally would be taken out, and then he would turn gold into crosses and so on, for the Red Berets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were there any guards at the TO warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a room. To the left from the entrance where we entered, there was a small room, and the guards were in there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Before I carry on, are you able to see the picture on your screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: While we're at this issue, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could you elicit from the witness who the guards were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I was about to do that. But I thought a picture was on the screen. Let me carry on then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us to which organisation the guards belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The guards -- well, they were mixed. They were police members but most of them were reserves. Not so many active-duty policemen who were involved doing their jobs. There were people I didn't know. There was a guy I knew well who was there often, Mihajlovic. He used to beat us. He would take us up to the office and beat the prisoners. They never took me up there, but they would be beating people all night long. It was wasn't always the same group of guards. They would rotate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the first name of this Mihajlovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Tomo Mihajlovic, nickname Kuka. Used to work for the garbage depot. He was in charge of the garbage depot in Teslic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were there any members of the paramilitary forces present at the TO warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes. Almost everybody used to come, Marijan Gacic used to come. He was a taxi driver but he was also a paramilitary, a difficult person. There were many people who had criminal records. Some of them were people who I used to arrest. All sorts of people. They would get assignments, I guess. There were guards around the building and there were guards in this room in the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So could you explain to the Court. You told us there were policemen, mainly reserve policemen. And you are telling now there are also members of paramilitary units. Do you know which paramilitary units we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were either volunteers or reserve troops that were sort of brought in by force. I also heard that there were prisoners there who were given weapons. Not only that I heard so, I -- on one occasion, there was a group of criminals that were brought to the check-point where I was earlier on, and then I refused to work there with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, maybe my question again was a little vague. Did you know the name of these paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew the names of the people, but not their formations or units. Whether they were part of a political party, parts of the authorities, members of the reserve police, or army, I wouldn't know. I know them as individuals. Some of them had military uniforms; some had whatever they wanted. They had all sorts of insignia. There were tricolour flags, come had kokades. It was all mixed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're telling us that there were some who had kokades and all sorts of insignia. Did any of these guards ever tell you to which paramilitary unit they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I assumed they were part of some group of volunteers. They never spoke about that. They only type of communication they had with us was through kicks and hits. I didn't ask them. I didn't dare ask them anything. I -- if I even looked them in the face, I would be beaten, so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic your intervention didn't come through on the transcript. Could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there were no problems concerning the transcript. I stood up to say that this was a leading question. The witness told us he didn't know and then the question came, Do you know what group they belonged to. The witness said, I know the names but not the groups they belonged to. And yet my colleague insisted on hearing the names of these units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: This is not a leading question to ask the witness what unit they belonged to. I don't see how that's leading at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the picture on the screen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is the Territorial Defence Staff building, at the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in which part of the building were you held?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was held at the ground floor. There are three windows on the left-hand side here on the photo. These windows were high up. We couldn't reach them. And there were bars, maybe one and a half metre, that you could use to open the window.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how large was this room?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was rather big, bigger than this room here. It was narrower than this room we are in, but it was longer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to estimate in any way, in terms of metres, how wide we're talking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was maybe 6 to 8 metres wide and maybe 20 metres long. I can't tell you more precisely. You can see the photo. It's from the beginning to the third window and then the whole width of the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, you told us that you recognised Tomo Mihajlovic. Could you tell the Court what he was wearing when you saw him at the TO warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was wearing reserve police uniform, because he was part of the reserve force, police reserve force. He had an automatic rifle. He had a pistol, a baton, and cuffs, everything. He would come very often, take people out, bring people in, beat people, take them up to offices upstairs, and they were calling people up throughout this time, all the times at night. But they never took me up. I don't know why not, but they didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time where Mr. Mihajlovic took you out of the TO warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe a month after I got there. And I was not interrogated at all. And then, on one occasion, he called out my name and Hasanovic's name and a reserve guy who was -- who owned a private company that -- for moving furniture and so on. There was Mr. Blagojevic also who was a reserve policeman, a nice guy. And Tomo Mihajlovic then unprovoked took this police baton out and hit me over the head about 15 times or so, and then Momir took this police baton from him and said try hit him one more time and then I'll hit you. And then Tomo turned to him and told him, you'll see what will happen to you now. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We didn't hear the name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But they were not doing anything out in the open, they were sending him [as interpreted]. And finally he took me to the SUP building, he and the driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Mihajlovic took you to the SUP building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was the escort and Jovan Kupresak was the driver. He's a nice guy. He is the brother of a colleague of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where in the police station did he take you to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is only one police station in Teslic, to the police station where I used to work. He took me to the first floor and left me there in the corridor. After barely a minute or two from the office where the secretary's assistant was, a man, short man, who had a dark green beret on his head and a scar above his right eye, he asked me who I was. I told him and he said, Hmm, you've come to the right place. You're not going to leave this place alive. So he went back in and after maybe 30 seconds or so, let's say seven men came, young men, in -- with sun-glasses, Italian, modern, and they wore camouflage uniforms and they had an eagle coat of arms which is a Serbian coat of arms, I think, on their left shoulder, and they started beating me, kicking me. One hold my leg and kept me against a wall and the others were hitting me. I tried to protect myself moving left to right, to avoid the worse blows. And in all this commotion somebody's eyeglasses fell and I stepped on them and they said -- one of them said, I'm going to kill you for this. But they then suddenly ran down the stairs and I was left lying there. And then the chief of the crime department, Milan Etic, picked me up, helped me into the room, and set me down into an arm chair. I apologise. And soon after that Pijunovic, Miroslav entered the room and he asked this Nedic, did he say anything? And Nedic said, No, no, he's fine. And then he hit me with his first with full force on my left-hand side on my face and I fell down, and then he cursed my mother said if he doesn't start talking I'll come in and slaughter him. And a moment after that, a colleague of mine entered, Marinko Djukic who was at the time assistant commander or something like. He was a young policeman who had worked with me before, and he walked in, started laughing. He used my nickname and said, Wouldn't you say that my guys know how to beat? And I said, Well, yes. And then he said, But this is nothing unless you start talking about the weapons and everything. And I told him, Okay. Milan, write it down, I'll -- I'll kill him personally. And -- or he said I'll kill him personally, but he said okay. You are now in power, you weren't so brave before but it seems you've changed. And then the first question they put to me -- that Milan put to me was about Odzak, when was it that I was there for the last time, and I responded I was never in Odzak, never in my life. I have passed by but I haven't been in the town. And he said, there are our guys there who have to graze the grass. We have information that you were there. But I said, no, I wasn't there. And then he asked me about the weapons. But earlier when I used to work as a part of the special police, the reserve police, I used to have hand grenades and such stuff and he asked me where that stuff is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: One correction for the transcript, it's page 41, line 23, 25 -- the witness mentioned that these guys wearing white belt. It is not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I was going to get back to them, actually. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were telling us about these gentlemen who came in in camouflage uniform with sun-glasses and eagle coat of arm. There's an intervention to the transcript, did you say something about -- did you say anything about a white belt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was white belt as worn by the military police. And they also had shoulder straps also white. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us about the eagle coat of arms. What is the significance of the eagle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That eagle was worn by members of the Serb army, the legal members of the Serb army. I, even now, see these insignia on the members of the army of the Republic of Serbia. It's legal now. But where they got it from at those times, I don't know. And they also wore the three colours of the -- the Serbian colours. Those were not Bosnian insignia. They were taking off all the red stars and kicking them about and putting on these other insignia with the Serbian colours instead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now is it fair to say that after your -- well, this event, you were taken back to the TO warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I was beaten there, I didn't know what was ahead. I wanted to jump off the van and start running because we were driving past a park. And I had a plan to go downstream and reach the Federation, but my fellow police officer didn't let me, he said he would shout. But on our way back, Momir, or, rather, Tomo Mihajlovic wasn't there, only the driver. He was a good guy and I thought he wouldn't shoot at me. So I didn't succeed. They didn't let us. I was brought back to the TO. They were all lying there beaten up and bloody and I was appalled, and Jozo said to me you faired well, look at me, but you will make it. You will escape. And they were all beaten badly on that day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, you were brought back to the TO warehouse and you told us that you were beaten at the police and before that you also told us that were beaten at the TO warehouse. Did anyone else beat you at the TO warehouse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not on that day. On the following day, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who did that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All sorts of people came there. They were sitting by the building drinking and I heard with my own ears. They said -- they were saying who was down there and they also mentioned my name, and they said, well, bring him, and then four or five or six of them would come and beat everybody, including me. They started kicking the metal door, then we all had to stand up and face the wall and raise three fingers and start singing the song "koto kaze koto laze [phoen]," and then they would pick the ones they wanted to beat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "they," did you find out who these people were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know one well by sight but I don't know his name. He was tall and had curly black hair. He entered and asked me -- or, rather, called my name and asked where I was. And I responded. He brought a stick from the Borja company, it was a timber processing company. He brought this stick and hit me on the head on -- and on my back two or three times, and I fell on the floor. And when I turned around I saw him. Then he hit me once again and I still have the scar here. Actually, two. And I bled badly. But the stick broke when he hit me on the head. Then he left. I heard that he got killed later somewhere. Then there was Sava Kostic's son. He once came with a chain taken off a chain-saw and he also had a leather glove. He beat me on the back with that chain, and my -- my skin was all torn and so was my shirt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the last name of this Sava?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kostic. His younger son Pero is -- actually, I know his son Pero who is a good guy, but the other is a problem, has always been a problem, and he had been brought in by the police several times and he was the one who beat me. Tomo Mihajlovic also entered but I only heard him. I didn't see him because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one second, please. Did there come a time when you saw a man by the name of Nebojsa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. On the first day when we were brought there Nebojsa entered and Piko did. Down at the detention unit there was Mirsad Gilic. I'm not sure about his first name, but he was a very nice guy, a Montenegrin. He was a teacher. We used to meet formally in pubs and so on. In the station they beat him with some wooden object. I don't know exactly what. Then Piko and Nebojsa came. They called him Srbo, he was from Serbia allegedly, and they said that he married a Radisic woman and took her to Serbia, and they called out his name, Gilic. He was all bloody and beaten and almost in a comma. And they were carrying a hammer with a long handle. It must have weighed a kilo or two. And they approached him. Piko took that hammer and swung his arm and he just raised his hand and said, No, please not with the hammer. But he hit him on the head with this hammer, and the hammer almost went through the skull. So he killed him on the spot and the guards entered and carried Gilic outside. Then Piko came, Saba Masinovic, the taxi driver was beaten up there. Saban --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, just one second please. Could I ask you to focus your answers to the specific question. And when I asking you about Nebojsa, could you tell the Court if you noticed anything about his uniform or any distinctive signs on him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wore something else every time. Most times he wore a police uniform and he said that he was an active-duty police officer. He wore a uniform hat with some insignia. But something else all the -- every time, and then he wore -- had different weapons on him, pistols or automatic rifles. But most times he wore a police uniform. For a while he had a "kokarde" on his hat and on his belt. So nobody was able to tell who he was with. They always called him Srbo or Nebojsa, but I'm not sure it was his real name. I was unable to learn anything more about him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did this Nebojsa ever speak to you and tell you to which unit he belonged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They never spoke to us about that. We were able to draw some inferences; that's all. But they wouldn't say anything about themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May I just have a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I just seek to refresh the witness's memory with one of his former statements, if that's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: On which issue, Mr. Demirdjian?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: On this issue of this individual we're just talking about and which unit he belongs to. It is in relation to adjudicated fact 1215.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You remember the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honours. Your Honours, just to clarify this. I just hand him the document directly and we don't show it on the screen, is that the procedure you were alluding to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, and invite him to read the relevant portion then ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. May I ask the usher to provide the witness with the statement he provided on the 29th of May, 2010.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, maybe ... on one occasion, he said that he was one of Arkan's Men. Maybe that's what you're alluding to. And he said, I'm one of Arkan's Men, I will kill you all. You have to do this or that. So -- but let -- maybe that's what you're interested in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't look at the statement sir, please. You can put it away. Okay. Let's carry on with this. He told you he was one of Arkan's Men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He told us all. He once came back and told us he was one of Arkan's Men. I don't know if it's true, but he said it anyway. And he said, you will remember me. You know who Arkan is. And we said, yes, we do. That's how it was. It's been a long time though. It's fortunate that I remember this much. Well, I may have forgotten some things though.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine, sir. And did you notice any patches on his uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, sometimes he had an eagle, another time he would have a -- that Serbian insignia. He dressed differently. You can see all sorts of things on him. It seems that he liked to dress up. But I think that he was more of a boaster than a real performer. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, outside this individual, do you know if other men from Arkan's group were present in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they called themselves that. When you were imprisoned down there, the guard who was a good guard, told us, be careful, Arkan's Men are here. Don't make noise. When they enter sing, you know what to do. If you make noise they will come and kill you all. That's what we were told. We all had to face the wall then we were beating us. If somebody turned around by chance as happened at the SUP, I once turned around involuntarily, and someone had entered. And another young boy turned around. And then they said, Turn around, you. And I wanted to turn around but then I heard a shot and they had shot the guy -- the other guy who had turned around. So even when they were beating us the one from the other end was able to see who was being beaten at the other end and vice versa. But who dared turn around? And it was only that way that we got information about who came there and who beat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Earlier, sir, you told us that you were detained in the TO warehouse until the month of August. What you did do after you were released from the TO warehouse.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing. It was limited. This Predrag Radulovic came, one of the members of the special units of the Serb army, the police. He went to Banja Luka. He found Predrag Radulovic and explained to him what was going on, that the so-called Red Berets are mistreating Serbs. The Serb military and the Serb police slapping them on the face in public, shooting, all sorts of things were happening. And then Predrag Radulovic got his groups of special units ready and one early morning we heard shots. There was fighting. And we assumed that it was either the HVO guys who had made their way to us or the Muslims, and we were glad. We expected to be set free. But then after a couple of hours the fighting stopped. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted). And he said what are you two doing here? Did anybody beat you? And I didn't dare say. So I said no, no, nobody. And he promised us he would release us. And after a few days --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: May we shortly go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, after you were released, where did you stay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had an apartment in Teslic. I also had a house; I mentioned it already. I didn't dare go there because everybody knew me well and everybody was armed. I told you, even former criminals carried weapons. And I even went to my house. Sometimes I stayed upstairs, sometimes downstairs, but I didn't dare move about. I was advised not to move about, and if I had to that I should inform the police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were out -- let me ask you, were you aware of the presence of the Serb Radical Party in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. There was the SDS, there were the radicals, there were various parties, especially in that pre-war period and during the war there were radicals too, and all parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know whether any armed group was related to the radicals in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The radicals had their own men, the group they were called Seselj's Men. I had no personal contact with them, but I heard of their existence. The so-called Seselj Men. There were the White Eagles, the Arkan's Men. That's what I heard from others. I didn't dare ask anybody who they belonged to. In Teslic you could find all the various formations that there were on the Serbian side. They were either locals or people from Serbia. There were vehicles from Serbia. Many soldiers arrived in trucks with Subotica or Novi Sad licence plates. Where they went, I don't know. Probably they were deployed in the hills and mountains around Teslic, but they would stop at Teslic and go to shops and pubs and after a short while they continued toward Banja Luka. Where exactly, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Page 51, line 12, the witness said I never had contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that, too. You're right. Yes, yes. Right after White Eagles and Arkan's Men, I never had contact with them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you told us that you knew of Seselj's Men and you knew of all these groups. You told us you already saw one man who claimed to be in Arkan's Men. Did you ever see any members of the White Eagles or Seselj's men in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did because they arrived in black jeeps. They had black flags or had the skulls. And they had white eagles on their sleeves, black uniforms. They were shouting, screaming, shooting. Croats and Muslims had to hang out white flags or sheets for them to know who we were. And then they would just fire bursts at our houses. They weren't people I knew, so I was afraid they would shoot me. So I removed that white flag and they didn't fire at my house anymore. But they did fire at the neighbours' houses. I heard the story. They stopped near my house, and I heard them say that there's nothing to loot here. Everything has been looted so we're leaving tomorrow. I heard them speak to each other because their two jeeps had stopped, and I never saw them again. On the following day they were gone. They probably came to loot or ... I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. The last topic that I'd like to deal with before the break, sir, is the following. You told us about the police station and the TO warehouse. To your knowledge were there any other detention centres in Teslic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Pribinic was some 15 kilometres ago [as interpreted]. That was one very nasty camp. Then there was Partisan in the very centre of Teslic. Partisan actually was a large gym with all you need for a workout. I apologise. Then at the Mladost school, Croats were detained. And it was mostly Muslims who were detained at Partisan. Then there was the Proleter sports ground. They had some changing rooms there. And also at Banja Vucica they were -- some people were locked up in the tennis courts. They also had some closed facilities there, and my brother was held there for a while before he was moved to where I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And how do you know about all these detention centres? You told us that you knew about your brother held in the last one. But about the others, how do you know about them being detention centres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know from speaking to people. A friend of mine, Jozo Mihic, he was detained with my brother. And then there was my brother and then there was a relative of mine and several friends, they were detained there for two or three weeks. And they actually received rather good treatment. They got food from home. But we faired very badly. Down at the SUP in the weapons storage, he was badly beaten up. My brother, I mean. Three ribs were broken. And then he was moved to where I was. And this young boy, Almir I think was his name, he wasn't even a teen. He was killed there that night. They beat him with all sorts of objects, sticks, kicking him. He lied beside me. He moaned all night, but then he died and in the morning he was carried out, dead. He was half Serb half Muslim. I think his mother was Muslim. He said that the Green Berets would come to the Teslic. That's a Muslim army, and allegedly that's why they killed him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well, sir. And one last question before I complete my examination. Out of all these ordeals you went through, can you tell the Judges what was the extent of the injuries that you sustained during your detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After I was released, my mother couldn't recognise me. She was standing next to me and calling my name. I was standing next to here. She couldn't see me. I came out with my hair grey, salt and pepper, rather. It was black before. I had to tie trousers around me so they wouldn't fall down, and I didn't have a shirt because it got torn by the beatings. I had a serious spinal injury. I didn't tell you about this. On one night they took me to a room and they were beating me with pipes, thick one-inch thick pipes, and one guy simply beat me until I lost any feeling in my legs. I fell down and they kept beating, and then they kicked me out of that room and all the way to where I was kept. I couldn't move. And three or four of them were dragging me to where I used to be. I didn't have any clothes on top and now have this asthma. I was immobile for about 15 days, and then Piko would come and walk over me and was saying, get up, get up, you can get up. They probably had some plans with me. Maybe to take me together with a group that was taken to Borja and killed there, but my brother heard because he was next to the door something and he said, Don't get up. So I stayed. I couldn't go -- to toilet. Four or five people were required to get me up and then I'd pee into a can and then they put me down and after I was released. On the left side of my spine I think there's some injury. I still feel it. I was all black and blue, even red, yellow ... well, my mother couldn't recognise me. I was standing next to her. I said, It's me. And she said, No, you're not my son. I was exhausted, hungry, thirsty. They were bragging, saying, Ustashas are making our people in this town grazing grass and we are bringing you mineral water. But, yes, they would bring mineral water but they would pee in it. And on the first day you don't drink, but it was really hot so on the next day I would. After I was released, later on I -- when I was abroad, I went for checkups and I was also told that I contracted syphilis, and I guess it must have been there. Or at least traces of that. And then they used antibiotics to cure me. I don't know what else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank, you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And this is a convenient point for us to take the break and we will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the witness is on his way back to the stand, there are two matters. One is that we remind the parties that we did not receive the progress report of last week on the matter of the -- the -- the stipulations. Counsel would recall that we expect ruling reports from them to know how we proceed. The second matter is that on the issue of photographs which may have been produced as a result of the site visit and the -- in large part, we would have heard what counsel would have had to say on this matter when the issue came of a particular photograph that was shown to the witness, that, bearing in mind the rule as to the conduct of site visits, that the -- if photographs are to be received into evidence which were only produced at that time, for the sake of compliance with the practice procedurally, they should only come in as a result of an application to add them in the first instance of the 65 ter list, which means that the settled rules as to additions to that list would be applied. And citing as an example the specific photograph in question, inasmuch as it appeared to us -- it appears, I should say, to us that the photograph in question is in a different form already on the 65 ter list without, of course, ruling on the -- on the specific application that in -- on any application to add it as a photograph that was produced at the site visit to the 65 ter list, counsel would have to -- would have to show why it should be substituted or added to a document that's already on the 65 ter list. So I trust that that clarifies matters and would guide counsel in future. To summarize, we aren't saying -- we aren't applying an absolute prohibition to matters produced during the site visit, but they could not go in otherwise than through the rule dealing with additions -- other than through the gateway, if I may call it that, of the 65 ter application.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may I pick up on that. So is it the position of the Trial Chamber that all the material that was gathered, the videos, the photos, the record, that will not be admitted on the record; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. And that was, we would have thought, well set out previously in -- not only in this case but in terms of the protocols developed by the Tribunal in terms of site visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And a second point. In relation to material of -- sorry, images of buildings that were not on the 65 ter list before, so I cite to the example of the building next to the SJB building. If we had no pictures in the past, I assume that category of pictures Your Honours might be more willing to, in as much as it assists, of course, the Trial Chamber in understanding, might be more willing admit that type of -- that category of photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. That's why we said we would not adopt a rigid approach of excluding anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- that only was produced as a result of the site visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And one last thing before we continue, I see that the statement that I sought to refresh to the memory of the witness with is still in front of him. Perhaps we could ask the usher to take it away, as he doesn't need it anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Aleksic, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. My name is Aleksandar Aleksic. I'm one of the Defence attorneys for Mr. Zupljanin. I have a few questions for you. But before that, I would like to say that I sympathize with you for all your sufferings. However, we are professionals here and we have to determine some facts that the parties find contentious, and I will have a few questions for you in order to determine them. You had several contacts with the OTP investigators. Your first statement was made on the 26th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, most probably. I didn't write the date down, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: After you gave the statement, the statement was read back to you in a language you understand. You signed it, thereby confirming that what's in the statement is according to the best of your recollection; is that correct? Could you please repeat your answer? The interpreters didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the 18th of October, 2000, you had another opportunity to read the statement and on that occasion you made some changes. Some of the changes were of typographic nature and there were other changes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember, but it's possible. So I said I don't remember, but it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And then this year, on the 28th and 29th of May, you met with my learned colleague. You gave another statement about the events. And you did have some changes and clarifications in relation to the first statement. The procedure was the same. The statement was read out to you in a language you understand, and then you signed it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: During the proofing yesterday, you also had some changes to your first statement. We'll come to that later. You stated that some parts of this first statement of yours were not correct and you wanted to verify.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every time I was giving statement I was responding to questions put to me. I did not read my previous statement every time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. And finally, do you remember having given a statement in 1998, a statement you gave to Ijdin [phoen] in Tesanj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did give a statement. I don't recall which agency it was. They told me it was state security, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In your previous statements and today during your testimony, you mentioned the meeting that took place -- the gathering, the meeting that took place in front of the police station in Teslic. You stated that there were politicians present, also some members of the army, and that the civilians who were there told you that a decision was reached that the Teslic public security station would come under the CSB in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. But it was deputy commander Mato Martinovic who told us that. They were at the meeting. The commander as well, Sabinko Mehmedovic and the chief at the time, Drago Kuzmo. There were other people. I don't know who was there from Banja Luka, but I did see also one or two people in military uniforms there. I cannot remember exactly how many of them there were there.
