Our senior officers were there, and the people from Banja Luka. And also from Doboj, from the CSB centre. I don't know them personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you know that up until the arrival of Mr. Radulovic and his appointment for position of the chief of SUP. So, in practical terms, until July, the SJB station did not come under the CSB.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't know who they were under. I know all the senior officers were replaced with Serbs. There was only one police officer but he just a police officer, regular policeman who was a Muslim. Otherwise, there were no Croats or Muslims in the leading structures, which means that they were removed. All the senior officers were Serbs from that moment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Today, you stated again that you were told after this meeting that you should go home and that you should not come to work anymore. However, in paragraph 6 of your statement -- of your 2010 statement, you said that, on that day, or maybe several days later, you were asked to sign a loyalty oath, and you all signed because you had no option.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct. I don't know when exactly that was, but I did sign it, this document of joining the force. They told us we won't be touched, that we should sign that we accept the Serbian authority, and we all signed it. I think we all signed it. I don't think anybody refused to sign it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In that same paragraph, you stated that non-Serb policemen were told that they would be called back to work after the takeover of power. Once that was completed, they would be called back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But those were just empty stories.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My colleague, Mr. Demirdjian, asked you what did you do after that. Is it correct that you went to Komusina and joined a HVO unit or some other unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Prior to that I had various contacts. I was searched. People wanted to beat me. They wanted to take away from me the weapons I had signed for, and then in late April I decided to go there. On my own initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: From what I've seen in your statements, you returned home on the 3rd of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, on the 4th of June, in the evening hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And you stated that the HVO unit's command post was in Komusina. Could you tell us, please, what was the name of the unit, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These were the residents of Komusina. My family is from that place, so they were defending the village. They weren't attacking. They just deployed. There were talks amongst Serbs in Teslic that they had tunnels and carrying out attacks, that they had black shirts and are very dangerous. But when I came up there, I realized that they had nothing. There was maybe one or two automatic rifle, otherwise it was hunting rifles. They didn't have anything but that. They were poorly equipped. Those were the locals. Now, there were people from HVO who would come and visit Komusina promising that they would send some kind of assistance, but they never did. It was only the locals defending their own village. However, they failed in doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You said that you took your automatic rifle there. It's not in the transcript. Can just confirm that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I took the automatic rifle and five clips of ammunition I signed for.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Now that we're discussing this topic, do you know that in other villages, Muslim villages such as Stenjak, that were Muslim units stationed there in this little area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no. These were no units. These were the inhabitants of Stenjak and Rankovaci. They did put up some resistance, resistance that lasted for about 20 minutes or an hour. There were no units there. These were just locals. And Stenjak is close to Tesanj, so they started firing only when they were fired upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that. Just a second. On page 4 of your first statement, you speak about the period prior to the events, and you say that foreign people would come to Tesanj offering weapons to Muslims and Croats and that the weapons were bought by people who were rich.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not Tesanj. That's Teslic. On one occasion I ways present when a man came to Jozo Martinovic, Rupa, who was a carpenter, offering him to buy a pistol or a rifle, and he looked at me and I gave him a sign, you don't need to do that so he refused, but some people did take the weapons. And when the Serbian police was set up, on that occasion, this Piko person and his group came because I know I had a friend who was part of that group, never mind who he was. And then they came to this person and asked, give me the rifle such and such a number. So it means that somebody had set up these men, that they told them who they selled -- sold -- who they sold these rifles to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You also spoke about the period of June or somewhat earlier, that the first shelling occurred of Teslic from the direction of Tesanj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Teslic was shelled but I don't remember the date. It's been 18 years. And when I gave my statement, I -- or statements I only answered questions and there were different questions every time. Sometimes I said something that I hadn't said before. Well, there was shelling anyway. And there was some makeshift shells were used and some didn't explode. One flew right past me, and a shell fell nearby but didn't explode. Those shells weren't properly manufactured.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, you said that was the first shelling. Now you say one shell fell and that was in September, when you left Teslic, which means that there was several instances of shelling, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I wasn't present. That's the only one I saw, this -- this shell. That was in September. And I heard that shells did fall there, and even some Muslims got killed in Teslic. Two guys. And one Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: One more question about this. Do you know from which positions these shells were fired?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How should I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: From Tesanj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, probably. I know that the Croats in the HVO didn't have any. They did have multiple rocket-launchers. They were in the direction of Zepce but they didn't have any shells probably due to the planes. No shells ever arrived there; I know that for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: And you said in your statements that you heard the shooting and the shelling, but since you were in your house you couldn't see what was going on in Stenjak particularly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Stenjak, the shooting started. I don't exactly remember when, and then tanks started advancing towards Stenjak and then they routed the enemy there and they all fled. But it went on for ten minutes or quarter hour, not more than half an hour anyway. Tanks started moving and the police and they simply overran those that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise. At page 63, line 16, the question includes the village the witness is from, and I'm not sure if we have any concerns here. I would prefer that we redact that just to be on the safe side, taking into consideration everything else the witness has said so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: It identifies. Yes. The name does not appear right now. There's a caret instead, but eventually it will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And Mr. Aleksic, may I remind you of the limitations of the scope of this witness's testimony. I think you are just on the borderline to exceed what this witness is supposed to testify about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I understood correctly, the witness has been called to testify about adjudicated facts 500 through 503. And the village I'm asking questions about is mentioned in that fact, the attack on that village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm not sure that this is entirely correct, Mr. Aleksic. The witness is supposed to shed some light on the parts of a couple of adjudicated facts which was redacted by the Chamber, and as far as facts -- adjudicated fact number 501 is concerned, the redacted part was about the involvement of the Bosnian Serb army and the police and the assistance by the paramilitary groups in the search of houses. And, as far as the other adjudicated fact is concerned, that is, adjudicated fact number 504, it also deals with the involvement of Bosnian Serb military police and regular police and reserve police and paramilitary forces in the detention of civilians. And then three other facts have been involved, that's 1214, 1215, and 1218, and none of these facts deal with the shelling of Teslic. But this was just to remind you to respect the limits of the testimony of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Sir, you said that your house is 3 and a half kilometres from Teslic, and you couldn't see which forces attacked Stenjak from where you were.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't see. But I heard as much from the people who were watching. People watched from their apartments. Their family, their friends --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: But you didn't see it personally.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. And I don't -- my vision is not that good. And apart from that, there was dust and smoke and -- so I don't know what could be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: About your stay, on page 7 of your statement from 1999, you said after Mr. Radulovic's arrival you were released from the TO building to go home. And you said that the first time around you were free for 15 days and so you then said that you were later forced to report to the Mladost school to do some work, and the guards occasionally mistreated and attacked you, but you were allowed to receive food from home. We were locked and set free for seven to eight days. When we were outside we were hiding and we tried to provide for our family. Yesterday, we were informed by the OTP that you wanted to change this part.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Just listen to me. I haven't finished yet. But that is the statement that you signed in a language you understand and it was read out to you confirmed and you still confirmed that it was truthful and accurate to the best of your recollection. Yesterday, you said it was not so, that you didn't have to go to Mladost and work there, and you said that you knew people who were held at Mladost in Pribinic but that you personally never went there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. I never went there. I don't know how that mistake happened. I can't have said that. I was speaking about a friend of mine who was also in Berlin in Germany. He was there, and I may have spoken about him and it was misunderstood. But I wasn't there. I was at the TO. And later they would call from me to come from home and then we went to Pribinic to put out the fire because the school was on fire. I knew that was Mladost but I never went there. This must be a mistake. I -- I'm -- I noticed yesterday and I said I never stated that. How it came about, I really don't know. But I wasn't kept there. I had nothing to do with Mladost. Some my colleagues and friends were there. I may have spoken about them or perhaps it was misinterpreted. This is really the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking. You had at least four occasions to correct that, and you only did it now, after this much time. But, okay, you gave an explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: A suggestion is being put that the witness had four occasion to correct that. He gave a statement and gave a supplementary statement in 2001 and that's the extent of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The statement from 1999, the correction from 2001, the statement from May this year, and yesterday's opportunity. That's four occasions, but the witness has explained and I'm satisfied.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I was never asked about the circumstances. I would never have said something that's not true. I had nothing to do with that. But there were people who were there, some relatives of mine, some friends, about a dozen people I knew, and they told me about it and based on what I heard from them I mentioned it and somebody put it down as my statement. But that's not correct. People did go through all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Concerning this, you said a short while ago that you were in your house, but -- after all these events. Yesterday you received a note that you were in your house basically in -- in home arrest, and there would be a police officer checking every day whether you were there. Today you testified differently. That you could have been in your apartment but you had reason to be afraid so you were in your house. So that means you were not under house arrest.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was. Every day, every morning somebody would come to see whether I was alive. They would send my colleagues to check on me, allegedly, but it -- it's clear why they came. The police had to be informed that I was there all the time. So there was no moving about town. No walking around.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] Until the beginning of June 1992, before the arrival of the Mice and all these people, what happened to you? And do you agree that when Mr. Radulovic came that they were all arrested and prosecuted and that order was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Part of that in pubs there was -- there were fights, brawls, and some people wore kokades, so there were fights on ethnic ground. The Mice arrived May and that's when the terror began. Among others, they even mistreated their own people. I think that they only arrived to loot and do whatever they felt like doing. And we were the ones who suffered from it. And once they were arrested things were fine. And let me explain you. Predrag Radulovic was there for a short while and then arrested in Belgrade for allegedly helping Muslims and Croats. And then it started all over again. The Mice were released, and they went back to their old ways. Not to the same extent, but ... and then they came -- that group came to my house to kill me at night --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll get there yet. So you said that when he arrived the condition significantly improved and that he apologised to you for what had been done to you, and you said after five or six days, you were all let go home and I -- he gave every one of you a sheet of paper and a pen asking you to put down what happened to you all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. And people asked me what they should do because they knew I was friends with him. And I said, be careful. It's better not to write anything because you don't know will happen. And, indeed, whoever put a complaint on paper later on disappeared and no one knows what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: All right. But for these reasons, you were formerly examined as a witness -- a witness and a victim in the proceedings against Piko and the others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where was I examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: In early June you gave a statement to the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Tesanj I gave a statement to the state police in Sarajevo. That's how they introduced themselves. Not to police, not to the court. They were inspectors from state security. Our former commander said to me that I should report on the following day, and then these guys came from Sarajevo and questioned me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: Do you know that proceedings were launched against Tomo Mihajlovic before the cantonal court in Zenica because of all these events.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I heard that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Could we have the year of those proceedings, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have that information ready but it's in my folder for the following witness. I don't believe that is a contentious issue. Perhaps a bit later I can provide a reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: One more detail. Today you spoke about how that man called Rambo was beaten up. And then you said that Piko lined up the police and ordered them to beat the man. And you also said whoever refused to beat him was beaten by Piko and his men.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. They were slapped and so on. Anyway, they were punished. Also, if one of the police officers carried a rifle without a -- without a strap, he would also be punished.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, won't you, when I say that Pijunovic and these people did whatever they wanted and that it was first and foremost them who terrorised the non-Serb citizens there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were the ones who inflicted the most evil upon everybody and caused the most problems. My house was burnt and some -- also some honest people were also dragged into this and made to commit crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: You only mentioned that Mr. Radulovic was removed from the post of chief of SUP. How do you know that, and how do you know that he was arrested?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once he disappeared I realized things started moving again. The worst things. And then I went to his brother's place, Nenad, who lived close by to myself and asked him, What's with Pile, because that was his nickname, and he said, Oh, my friend, they arrested him, put him in Hotel Yugoslavia under house arrest. He cannot move from there. That's what his brother told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: I have a few more questions related to your retirement. You told us it was upon your request because you have met the conditions prescribed by the law. Could you please tell us do you know -- or maybe it would be better if we moved to private session for a question or two.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: My name is Slobodan Cvijetic and I'm one of the Defence team members for Mr. Stanisic. I don't have any new topics. I will just ask for a few clarifications related to what you'd said so far. Today you told us about the appearance of those trucks that were supposed to take away the archives of the Territorial Defence. Do you remember discussing this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: If it's not a problem for you, could you please elaborate for the Trial Chamber. I will not put any questions to, and if you omit something, I'll put an extra question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't very much interested in what was going on. And I wasn't in Teslic at the time, but Mojo Colic, Asim Colic, and Emko Colic, these were guys who were doing all sorts of things and also Remzija Jasarevic, Budzo, he was maybe the most vocal of them. And there was also Rambo. There were these guys and some other guys. They went there to prevent them from taking the archives out. Because one could see that something was going on. Serbs were being armed and nobody's paying any attention to us in that respect. And these people just wouldn't allow them to cart that away. But all of them who were -- who took part in that, were the first one who were killed. Rambo, for instance, then also Budzo. Many of them. So they shouldn't have done it. Had they known about it they would have gone out of Teslic and they would still be alive today. And another guy -- oh, no this guy who was killed, Rambo, he was at the check-point in Barici, the check-point that was set up by the Muslims and Predrag Markocevic, commander during the wartime. He wasn't my commander --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: That's not necessary. My question was only related to the archives being transported away. So, please, stop here, and let me put you a different question. It was the members of the JNA who arrived to take the files of the conscripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's hard to tell. There were people in civilian clothes but in a military truck with JNA licence plates. I saw him, there was commotion, and then they left, I think, afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And the group that prevented them from transporting the documentation, according to the names, they were all Bosniaks, Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there were a few Croats. A guy that was killed, I think his name was Cinci from Barici, he was also killed. I don't know whether it was because of that and then a waiter called Tabak. He managed to survive because he ran to Komusina. There were a few Croats there who were there, simply who found themselves in the front of the TO and they just wouldn't let them remove the files. They must have known what may happen in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Sir, at the time, and in the times immediately before that, or to be more precise, during the times of the war in Croatia, the JNA was mobilising conscripts from the area. Was that not the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. But they would only take Serbs, as far as I know. No members of other ethnicity. I know only of Salkanovic, Ibrahim, who stayed within the police force, but he had to make some special kind of loyalty oath. He told me about it, but I'm not sure what exactly it involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Did Muslim and Croat conscripts respond to call-up? In brief, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Once we've signed the loyalty oath, we -- it meant that we accepted it, but nobody called us anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: This call-up for mobilisation was done on the basis of the very documentation that the JNA tried to take away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I know that this Nenad went there, took a semi-automatic rifle, uniform, a backpack, and asked him, What's all that? And he said, Well, I had to sign for it. I didn't understand it. Nobody called me. Nobody gave me a chance.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Talking about the man who was at the head of this group, Remzija Jasarevic, the most vocal according to you, you said he got killed in the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, he was killed in the camp, in Pribinic, not Pravilovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: I'm reading this from your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no, that's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Give me an opportunity to put it to you. It says here that he died in the war. So what's -- where's the mistake?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. That is a mistake. I wouldn't have mentioned him had he gotten killed in the war. That person did have criminal proclivities, yes. He would provoke people into fighting with him, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Why did you then tell the OTP that he got killed in the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say that. It must be a mistake. I wouldn't be mentioning him had he got killed in the war. There were so many people who got killed in the war, and I never paid attention to that. But that man, he was certainly killed, murdered. That's one of the persons I mentioned as murdered individuals. That must be a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Well, let me quote it to you, and you tell me whether this is correct: "Remzija Jasarevic, Budzo" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Budzo.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: "... a Muslim was the most vocal person in expressing his opinion and inciting crowds."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: He later got killed in the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not correct. I didn't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise. The copy of the statement that I have here, it just says "killed during the war." I don't know if it is a mistake in the translation. The English version here says "during." I don't know if that makes a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll give the ERN page number that's my reference. It's the statement of 26 March 1999. The ERN number is 0091-2274.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Then tell us, sir, what you believe. What's true what you said in 1999 or what you're saying now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm telling now that the man was murdered. I wouldn't have mentioned his name if he had been killed in the war. Many of them were killed in the war, and I mentioned none of them. I mentioned him as the one who was murdered. That's why. He was taken out of the camp in Pribinic and murdered up there. They beat him, tortured him and later killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You heard a quotation of your statement, so how do you explain that the statement given to the OTP in 1999 should read this way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't have said that. My memory was still fresh at the time. I can't have said that. How the mistake occurred, I don't know. I know as much as you do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not dwell on this anymore. You mentioned the changing of the street names, right? You said that happened immediately before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: After the multi-party elections, there were also changes of street names. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Why should anybody change that? Why should they change the name of the Marshal Tito Street? Everybody loved him and held him in high esteem. Only when the new authorities were established then there were these new inscriptions, the new graffiti that nobody removed, and that's how it was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But I put it to you that the change of the street names ensued immediately after the multi-party elections and that it was a process that went on until the war started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went there often before the war. I was stopped at check-points. I was searched. They were saying, We have to search every time --

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Just tell me, is what I have just put to you correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: You said that you had problems that you were a bit late because there was that curfew. But, sir, even Serbs who didn't respect the curfew had the same problems, did they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't believe they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: But do you believe it or know it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know it. It happened often and I know -- I know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: And I put to that you the curfew applied to everybody and that the Serbs who didn't respect the curfew had the same problems. Just tell me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a Serb colleague who was there before me and nothing happened to him and when I arrived, they want to the kill me.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No more questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Anything in re-examination, Mr. Demirdjian?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: On the issue of the shelling that my learned friend was asking you about from the Muslim or Croat forces, you told us that there was a shell that fell but that didn't explode, and that they were not properly manufactured. How frequently did you see these type of shells?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only once. And it flew past me only a few metres away from my nose and it fell in a marshy area. But I heard from people that shells fell on Teslic and Banja Vrucica and that they are probably produced by hand. And many of them didn't explode. Some of them fell on Teslic and some people got killed. Dr. Parovic, a Serb member of the Serb Radical Party lost a son, and the son of a baker, a Muslim, was -- was also killed in the shelling. I don't know what happened to the craters of those shells that fell on Banja. They may have -- they may have repaired that. But the shells didn't hit the target. They just fell all over the place [Realtime transcript read in error "police"]. And there was a filter factory in Tesanj and that's where they were making them. But they were short of [indiscernible] screws -- screws -- or, rather, these screws and nails, and what have you, to make these shells so they didn't have the appropriate material.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, there's a couple of interventions in the transcript. 79, 9, I believe the witness said instead "of many of them didn't explode," he said many of them were not -- were not able to hit the target. That is what he said later. And page -- line 13, "they just fell all over the place," not "the police." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: However, I remember hearing many of them didn't explode and many of them didn't hit the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: But, sir, you may want to clarify this with my next question. How frequent were these type of shellings, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Rare. I heard that they were fired from Tesanj when I was no longer there. But as I said, I only heard of that. I heard explosions when I was there and then I heard that somebody may have got hurt. In Teslic, one fell on the tarmac and pierced the tarmac but didn't explode. That happened too. And that happened after I had left Teslic, I really don't know. I only heard stories from others that this man was killed or that man was killed and those shells even killed some Muslim, so they killed their own people. I mentioned this one man but there were more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: All right. You asked about detention at Mladost and the clarification you provided us, and you told us that you didn't have to report to Mladost. Did you have to report anywhere at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: While Radulovic was there, I didn't have to. He would have even come to see us up there. But he said, Don't walk around, please. But only when he was replaced, I had to report daily or they would come to me and to check and asked me, Where you here? Okay, stay put. And sometimes here, sometimes there, but they always had to know where I was so that they could find me. So I wasn't allowed to hide. They supposed that I would cross over to the other side and then go berserk.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you said they would either check or you would have to report. Where did you have to report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The SUP, the police station. I had to report to the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You were asked at page 68 about the Mice and the fact that they came to loot, and it was suggested to you that they were doing whatever they wanted. Were you able to observe their relationship with the local Serb police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they seized power and they didn't report to anyone. There was talk that they were Milosevic's men. So they were -- the -- the authority on the ground. They could kill whoever they wanted, and whoever stood up to them faired very badly. No matter whether it was Serb or a Croat. But mostly it was us non-Serbs who suffered. They would come up and they didn't like something or there was a curfew, and then they would meet a police officer and they would snarl at him, What are you doing here? And slap him on the face. And one colleague of mine was even shot at when he was going home from his shift at night. On a high-rise apartment building there was a machine-gun position, and somebody thought he was suspicious and shot at him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You told us this morning that during the beating of Rambo, Kopic, in front of the police station by Piko that Markocevic was standing on the steps laughing. And that is what I want to ask you, what do you know of the relationship between the police and the Mice group?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness has answered the question stating that they had absolute power. This is too leading. This witness said he was standing there. I asked him something else. This is really leading. And the witness has said what they were doing. I don't have to read out the entire answer, I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: First, the answer he gave to my first question didn't answer the question. That's why I need to have an answer to this question. What was the relationship between these two units, these two organisations? It's a straight-forward and non-leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, could you answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I started speaking about that man Rambo. But I was stopped by counsel. He said that he would deal with that later. If you're interested I can tell you. This man Kopic, well, check-points had been set up, principally because of Predrag Markocevic. The Muslims had a check-point at Barici. If you go toward Banja Luka, you had to go through the village of Barici. And the Muslims had sort of a check-point there. And Predrag Markocevic was a police commander. He went to that check-point to see what it was about. And then that man Rambo and some other people pointed their rifles at him and sent him back, and he said, Don't you know who I am, the commander. They said, We don't care. Go back. And that's why Predrag stood by while he was being beaten up. And I heard that he was present when he was killed in the -- on the premises of the committee, because he was screaming all night and groaning. I even heard that Marinko Djukic and Predrag were present when he was killed. That's what I heard. So that's the reason why Predrag was laughing and was -- looking on, because they had sent him back from that check-point with him at gunpoint. And the relationship between the police and the Mice was a good one. I heard that the Mice were brought by Nikola Perisic, the president of the municipality, Savo, the priest, and others, the president of the SDS, Bogoljub Misic, they accepted the Mice. And they co-operated with them, because how could they have known me? Somebody must have assisted them. So there were good relations between them. But they were mostly taking it out on little people. Police officer comes by, doesn't carry his rifle, strictly according to regulations, and then they slap him and mistreat him. But, basically, they were on good terms with the authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, it's past the time when we would rise for the day. How much longer do you expect would be with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let me see. Your Honours, I only have two questions, so I could try to wrap it up right away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, in order to release the witness today, if we could move rapidly, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked about the trial of Tomo Mihajlovic. Did you know that it was held in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. That was the story.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber where is Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Zenica is between Sarajevo and Doboj, 70 kilometres from Teslic. Actually, 100. It's 30 to Doboj, plus 70, that makes 100 kilometres from Teslic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And is it correct that Zenica is part of the BiH Federation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I just have one final question for you before release you, and that relates to the Mice Group. Counsels on both sides have put questions to about relations between the Mice Group and other groups, and my question goes to your knowledge of the relations between the Mice Group and the Red Berets. Are you able to shed some light on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's the same group. But they had -- they were referred to by two names, the Mice or the Red Berets. But it's one and the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we thank you for your assistance to the Tribunal. On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I echo Mr. Aleksic's expression of sympathy for what you have suffered. You are now released as a witness, and we wish you a safe journey back to your home. Yes. So the usher could escort the witness -- I think we have to close the shades so that we take the adjournment in open court. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too. I wish you much success in your work. And I hope we won't see each other again, unless we have to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It has been brought to our attention that we were so successful in the -- keeping the witness' identity secret that his pseudonym doesn't appear on the record, so the record should be corrected to reflect the pseudonym that was assigned to him. 253.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: 253, yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we could raise the shutters. We are grateful to the interpreters and the reporters for the extra time that we would have spent in order to facilitate the completion of this witness. And we take the adjournment, to reconvene in this courtroom tomorrow morning at 9.00.
